The Torah is the central and most sacred text of Judaism, comprising the first five books of the Hebrew Bible: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy. Also known as the Pentateuch or the Five Books of Moses, it contains the foundational narrative of the Jewish people, cosmic origins and divine law, as well as the six hundred thirteen commandments, known as mitzvot, that govern Jewish practice and ethics. Believed by traditional Judaism to have been revealed by God to Moses at Mount Sinai, it forms the bedrock of Jewish theology, law, and identity. Its status as the most authoritative Jewish text—above even the Talmud—shapes its central role in Jewish ritual, study, and spiritual life. Its narratives and laws have profoundly influenced Western culture, law, and ethics through Judaism, Christianity, and Islam.

The Torah is composed of five books: Genesis, which covers creation and the patriarchs; Exodus, which tells of slavery and liberation; Leviticus, which contains priestly law; Numbers, which covers the wilderness wandering; and Deuteronomy, which presents Moses's final teachings. It contains six hundred thirteen commandments divided into positive precepts, instructing to do something, and negative precepts, prohibiting actions. These cover ritual, ethical, and civil law. The narrative arc spans from creation through Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Moses, concluding with Moses's death on the brink of the Promised Land.

The Torah has been transmitted orally for centuries before written transcription. In synagogue, it is read from a Sefer Torah, a scroll hand-written on kosher parchment by a trained scribe known as a sofer. The scroll is stored in the Holy Ark and handled with a pointer called a yad to avoid touching the sacred parchment. It is divided into fifty-four weekly portions called parashot, completing the annual cycle on Simchat Torah, meaning "Rejoicing in the Torah."

Traditional Judaism holds that Moses received both the Written Torah and the Oral Torah, interpretive traditions later recorded in the Talmud, from God at Mount Sinai. The Documentary Hypothesis, a major school of biblical criticism, proposes that the Torah was compiled from four source texts dated to the ninth through fifth centuries BCE. The Torah's influence radiates outward: the Ten Commandments form the basis of Western legal codes; the narrative of the Exodus became a metaphor for liberation in political and literary tradition; and the Torah's ethical and monotheistic vision shaped both Christianity and Islam.
